p: Ochoa's office was at the far end of the fourth floor hall from Maria's, and at 7:30 on a Tuesday in February the sun hadn't cleared the parking garage yet. Maria put the chart on his desk before she sat down. Rawlins, month by month, counting every dose. Ninety in December 2025. Sixty-four in January. Then a year in the low sixties.

The restated report had gone to the board's quality committee the day before, Laramie's 97 printed beside its 81 and Rawlins' 98 beside its 62, with a paragraph on Laramie's button and nothing yet on Rawlins. The committee had asked hard questions for forty minutes, most of them about Laramie. Nobody could answer why Rawlins fell, because nobody had looked.
Ochoa read the chart the way he read everything, all the way through, including the footnote. Then he took his glasses off.
Ninety-eight, every month, he said. Who signed it?
Nobody signed it. It was a report. It ran on the first of the month and went out to a list.

That's worse. He put the glasses back on. Tomorrow Aisha brings her sepsis alert to your council. She wants a machine that watches every patient and tells the nurse when to worry. I'm for it. But look at this first. This is what a number does when nobody checks what it's counting. An alert's a number too, and this one shows up on the nurse's screen.
He slid the chart back across the desk. Find out why January. Then go build Aisha's thing like you mean to measure it.
Ochoa's Legal Pad: the machine that taps you on the shoulder.

The Sunday before the pilot went live, Ochoa bought breakfast at the Greeley diner and drew a box on the legal pad with a lot of arrows pointing at it. Everybody thinks decision support means a pop-up, he said. The pop-up is the loudest kind, and usually the worst.

Clinical decision support, CDS, is anything in the system that helps a clinician make a better decision at the moment of care. Alerts and reminders are one kind. So are order sets, documentation templates, dose calculators, reference links, and a sepsis column on the unit census board. Some CDS interrupts: a pop-up the user has to answer before going on. Some is passive: it's there when you look, and it doesn't stop you. A hard stop blocks the action entirely. A soft stop lets the user override it with a reason. Hard stops belong to a short list of things that should never happen, because when a hard stop is wrong, nobody can get around it.

The test for any CDS is the five rights. Give the right information, to the right person, in the right format, through the right channel, at the right time in the workflow. A sepsis warning that goes to the dietitian fails the second one. A dose warning that shows up after the order is signed fails the last one. An alert that says possible sepsis and nothing else fails the first, because it doesn't say why or what to do next.

How the exam asks it. When a question describes CDS that isn't working, find which of the five rights it misses. The best fix usually changes who gets it, when, or in what form, before it adds another alert.

Ochoa wrote a number on the pad and circled it. In most hospitals, most interruptive alerts get overridden. Some of those overrides are right. Alert fatigue is what happens when users see so many alerts, so many of them useless, that they stop reading any of them, including the one that matters. The fix is fewer, better alerts.

So you measure. The override rate is overridden alerts divided by alerts fired. Count alerts per patient and per user per shift, too, and read the override reasons. A high override rate isn't automatically bad. If the patient was already being treated, overriding was the right call and the alert was redundant. Pull a sample and check whether each override was appropriate before you decide what the rate means.

Then govern it. Every alert should have a clinical owner, a reason to exist, a measure of whether it works, and a review date. Changes go through the same change control as any build, with testing. Alerts nobody owns, and alerts that fire constantly and change nothing, get retired. An alert is a promise you make to a nurse, he said. Every bad one teaches her not to believe the next.

How the exam asks it. High override rates point to design and governance, not to staff discipline. Expect answers about reviewing override reasons, retiring low-value alerts, and putting new CDS through a committee with an owner.

He drew a square and split it in four. Across the top, did the patient really have sepsis, yes or no, decided by a reviewer looking at the whole chart. Down the side, did the alert fire, yes or no. True positives fired and had it. False positives fired and didn't. False negatives had it and got no alert. True negatives had nothing and got nothing.

Sensitivity is TP divided by TP plus FN: of the patients who had it, how many did the alert catch. Specificity is TN divided by TN plus FP: of the patients who didn't, how many did it leave alone. Positive predictive value, PPV, is TP divided by TP plus FP: when it fires, how often is it right. Negative predictive value is TN divided by TN plus FN.

Aisha will look at sensitivity, Ochoa said. The nurse lives in PPV. Lowering a threshold catches more cases and raises sensitivity, and it fires on more people who are fine, so specificity and PPV fall. PPV also depends on how common the condition is. The same alert on a unit where sepsis is rare will be wrong more often, even though nothing about the alert changed.
How the exam asks it. Expect to build a two by two table from a story and compute all three. Know the tradeoff: a lower threshold raises sensitivity and lowers specificity and PPV.

A before and after comparison of two averages can fool you. Plot the measure over time instead. A run chart plots each week's value in order with a median line. A run of six or more points in a row on one side of the median is a shift, and five or more going the same direction is a trend. Either is a signal that something changed. Three good weeks aren't a signal yet. A control chart adds a mean and upper and lower control limits, usually three standard deviations out. Points inside the limits are common cause variation, the normal noise of the process. A point outside them, or a non-random pattern, is special cause, and it's worth investigating.

Use three kinds of measures, for an alert or for any new technology, like telepharmacy for a small hospital or remote monitoring for rural patients. Outcome measures are what the patient feels, like sepsis deaths or ICU transfers. Process measures are what the team does, like time to antibiotics. Balancing measures watch for harm somewhere else, like more broad-spectrum antibiotics or more nurse time spent on alerts.

How the exam asks it. When a question asks whether a change worked, choose the answer that compares against a baseline over time and applies run or control chart rules. Judge telehealth and telepharmacy the same way: the gap it closes, plus a balancing measure for the risk it adds, like a slower urgent dose.

And when your council splits, don't vote yet, Ochoa said. Start with what everyone already agrees on, usually the problem and how you'd know it's solved. Then design a test both sides can accept: a time-limited pilot, measures agreed up front, and a stop rule. Consensus is a decision everyone can live with. A vote taken too early settles the question and keeps the fight.
How the exam asks it. For a meeting in conflict, pick the answer that finds common ground and a fair process before any vote, mandate, or side taken by the chair.

Rules like Aisha's are written by people. Predictive models are trained on past data and give a score, like the chance a patient becomes septic in the next six hours. A vendor will quote a number like area under the curve from other hospitals. That number belongs to those hospitals. Validate the model on your own patients before anyone acts on it, often by running it silently and comparing its scores with what actually happened.

After go-live, keep watching. Models drift. The data going in changes, like a new lab analyzer with a new code. The patients change. Practice changes, often because of the model itself. Monitor performance on a schedule, by site and by group, and have an owner who can retrain or retire it. The FDA regulates some CDS software as a medical device. Software that lets a clinician independently review the basis for its recommendation is generally treated differently, one more reason to show your work.
Ochoa paid the check and tore the page off. A tool that taps a nurse on the shoulder had better be right more often than it's wrong. And you'd better know which it is.
How the exam asks it. For a vendor's predictive model, the best answer validates it locally before use and monitors it after. Published accuracy from other sites isn't evidence for yours.

Kiran had four files by nine o'clock, and none of them had been built to talk to the others. The eMAR, with every Rawlins dose and how it was charted. The dispensing cabinet's log of every override pull. Pharmacy's staffing schedule, by shift, for two years. And the safety event reports, which nurses filed in a separate system that used its own patient numbers.
I can put them side by side, he said. They don't share a key, and they don't agree on what a day is. Pharmacy's day starts at seven in the morning. The cabinet's starts at midnight.
Ochoa's question was still on the legal pad at the top of her page. Why January.
A. Report the pharmacist's retirement as the cause, since the dates line up so well.
B. Wait for three more months of data, so the cause is certain before anyone acts.
C. Ask the Rawlins nurse manager to audit her nurses' scanning, shift by shift.
D. Join all four on patient and hour with pharmacy, then check with Rawlins.

Kiran and a pharmacy analyst put all four on the same clock and the same medical record number. It reads plainly once it's lined up. Rawlins' last night pharmacist retired in January 2026, and the job was never filled. After five o'clock, nurses pulled first doses on cabinet override, and those orders weren't verified yet, so there was nothing on the eMAR to scan against. Nurses charted them with the Given, no scan button. Override pulls went from about 40 a month to over 600. By spring the button was a day shift habit too. Maria calls Gail before anyone else sees it. Gail is quiet a long time. So it was us. It was a hole, Maria says. Nobody showed you where it was.

That's the move. Disparate data sets only answer a question once they share a key and a clock. Join them on patient and time, look for what changed when the measure changed, and confirm the story with the people on the floor before you call it a cause.

The Clinical Informatics Council met Wednesday in the big room on the second floor, twenty-two people and a speakerphone for Wyoming. Aisha presented for twelve minutes without notes. Sepsis was killing people on Cascade's medical floors, mostly patients who got worse slowly, overnight, after they'd been admitted for something else. Her alert would watch every inpatient and fire when the vital signs and labs said sepsis was starting. She wanted it live in all eleven hospitals on March 1.
The ED medical director spoke first. My triage nurses screen every patient for sepsis already. Put one more pop-up in front of them and they'll click through all of them, this one included.
Greeley's director of nursing spoke next. My nurses get forty alerts a shift now. I've counted.
Forty alerts aren't a reason to let people die of sepsis, Aisha said. The room split down the middle and stayed there. Maria was co-chair, and every face had turned toward her end of the table.
A. Back Aisha as co-sponsor, and ask the room to trust the evidence she cited.
B. Call a vote now, since the council has a quorum and everyone's had their say.
C. Agree on the problem and the measures, then propose a short, measured pilot.
D. Send it to a small work group to return next month with a recommendation.

Maria writes three questions on the whiteboard. What problem are we solving? How will we know it worked? What would make us stop? The room fills the board in twenty minutes: time from sepsis criteria to antibiotics, alerts per nurse per shift, override rate, and a stop rule if nurses report harm from it. Then she proposes thirty days at Greeley, the ED and two medical units, 4 West and 5 East. The ED director crosses his arms. If you'll count my overrides honestly. Every one. Aisha looks at the board a long time. Thirty days.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Facilitating a split room means finding what everyone agrees on first. Here that's the problem and how to measure it. Then a time-limited pilot with a stop rule lets both sides test their worry instead of arguing it. Consensus is a decision everyone can live with, including the people who'd have chosen differently.
Thursday afternoon Kiran showed her the build in the Corvane test system. He'd built it in January from Aisha's spec, nights and weekends, and he'd tested it against two hundred fake patients.

Sepsis alert, version one, as specified. Fires when a patient has two or more of these within six hours. Temperature over 38 or under 36. Heart rate over 90. Breathing rate over 20. White blood cell count over 12,000 or under 4,000. Shows as a pop-up to every nurse and physician who opens the chart while the criteria are met. Must be answered before the chart opens. Choices: Will evaluate, or Not clinically indicated.

Every time, Kiran said. Anybody who opens the chart. A patient who meets it at noon gets it from the nurse, the doctor, the respiratory therapist, the next nurse. And it doesn't say which numbers set it off. He'd run it against a week of real 4 West vitals in test. It would have fired on a third of the unit.
A. Keep it for everyone who opens the chart, but let each person dismiss it for a shift.
B. Fire once to the patient's own nurse and doctor, show why, and link the order set.
C. Make it a hard stop that blocks the chart until someone orders a lactate level.
D. Make it a column on the unit census board instead, with no pop-up at all.

Kiran rebuilds it Friday. It goes to the assigned nurse and the attending physician, it lists the values that triggered it, and it opens the sepsis order set in one click. If the criteria still hold twelve hours later, it fires again. Aisha reads the new version and frowns. The respiratory therapist sees things too. Then she tells the nurse, Maria says. Like she does now.

Exactly right. Apply the five rights. The right people are the ones who can act. The right information says why it fired. The right format puts the next step one click away. An alert that explains itself and makes the right action easy gets read.

Friday morning Aisha emailed Maria and Kiran at 6:02. Since the pilot units would already be watching their alerts, she wanted to turn on five more with the sepsis alert. Acute kidney injury. A missing clot prevention order. A fall risk reassessment. An early warning score. Opioids ordered with a benzodiazepine. All built. All evidence based. Same thirty days, same units. Efficient.

Kiran pulled the inventory before he answered. Greeley already ran 386 active alerts. A hundred and fifty-eight of them had no named owner. Nobody had reviewed any of them in three years. One fired on every patient over 65 and had been overridden 99 percent of the time since 2021.
A. Put each one through council intake with an owner, a measure, and a review date.
B. Approve all five, but on two other units, so the sepsis data stays clean.
C. Hold all five until the pilot is over, then decide which ones to add next.
D. Turn all five on with the sepsis pilot, since those units are already set to watch.

Each of the five gets a one-page request: what it's for, who owns it, how it'll be measured, when it'll be reviewed. The council takes them one at a time over the spring. Kiran adds a second list: the 158 alerts with no owner. Aisha takes it in good humor, mostly. Fine. Give me the over 65 one. I'd like to kill it personally.

That's the move. Decision support content needs ongoing governance: an intake process, a clinical owner, evidence, a measure, a review date, and a way to retire what doesn't work. Use the same process for what's already live.
The pilot went live Monday, February 8. Friday morning at 6:10 Maria's phone rang, and the voice on it hadn't changed in eighteen years.

Bev Hart was charge nurse in the Greeley ICU that night. A sixty-eight-year-old retired rancher from Kersey had come up from 4 West at 5:30, admitted two days before for pneumonia. The sepsis alert fired at 1:40 AM. Heart rate 104, temperature 38.4. His nurse had answered it Not clinically indicated. At 4:50 his blood pressure fell, his lactate came back at 4.6, and the rapid response team took him upstairs.
He's on pressors and he's talking, Bev said. He'll probably be fine. His nurse is in the 4 West break room. She's first year. She hasn't stopped crying.
A. Ask the nurse manager to handle it with the nurse, and look at the alert later.
B. Turn the alert off on all three pilot units until the safety review is finished.
C. Require a second nurse to cosign every override of the sepsis alert from now on.
D. File the safety event, then sit with the nurse and her manager, and listen.

She files it from the parking lot at 6:40 and names the alert as a possible contributing factor. Then she goes to 4 West. The nurse is Brooke, twenty-three, eight months out of school. Hers was the ninth alert of the night, and the eight before it were nothing. He said he felt fine. He was talking about his cows. Maria listens all the way to the end. Then she says, My first year, I got lucky once. I'd rather build you something that doesn't need luck. Kiran pulls the log for the whole shift by eight. Bev texts at noon: he asked for his hat.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. A patient safety event involving CDS has to be reported, even when the patient recovers. Report it, and treat the alert as part of what gets reviewed. Talk to the nurse the way just culture asks: to learn, not to blame. Her nine alerts are data about the design.
Aisha worked a hospitalist night shift at Greeley the next Tuesday. She came to Maria's office Wednesday morning still in scrubs, with her coffee untouched.

I got my own alert nineteen times last night, she said. Post-op fevers. A man with a heart rate of 110 since 2019. A woman who was already on antibiotics for exactly this. I overrode eleven of them without reading past the first line. Eleven, Maria. I wrote it.
She set the coffee down. Pull it. I was wrong.
A. Leave it unchanged for the full thirty days, so the pilot data stays clean.
B. Keep the pilot, write up her night, and bring changes through change control.
C. Have Kiran raise the heart rate and temperature thresholds tonight.
D. Pull it today, since the CMIO who wrote it is now the one asking for it gone.

Maria has her write down all nineteen. Three patterns fill the page: fresh surgical patients, known chronic tachycardia, and patients already being treated. One change is small and safe, so it goes to Thursday's change board: no repeat firing while the sepsis order set is active. Kiran tests it that night. The rest waits for Monday's data. Aisha reads the list back to herself. I wanted to be the one who fixed sepsis. You still might, Maria says. Just not by Thursday.

Exactly right. Decision support improves through a loop: use, feedback, analysis, tested change. Frontline experience, even the author's, is the best feedback there is. Capture it, fix what's safe through change control, and let the data decide the rest.

Monday, February 22. Aisha's two residents had reviewed the chart of every patient on the three pilot units for the first fourteen days, all 1,200 of them, and decided by hand who had really been septic. Kiran matched their answers to the alert log.
Forty patients had sepsis. The alert caught thirty-eight of them. It also fired on 342 patients who didn't.
Ninety-five percent, Aisha said. It found ninety-five percent of them.
Greeley's director of nursing was on the call. And when it fired, it was wrong nine times out of ten.
They were both right. Aisha had one more proposal: lower the threshold to one criterion, so it would catch the two it missed.
A. Test a tighter rule on the same patients, and weigh what it misses.
B. Lower the threshold to one criterion, so it catches the two it missed.
C. Keep the rule, and tell the nurses that one alert in ten is a real catch.
D. Report sensitivity alone to the council, since it's the number Aisha trusts.

Version two needs two vital sign criteria plus a lactate of 2 or more or a new sign of organ damage. On the same 1,200 patients it catches 36 of the 40, misses 4, and fires on 84 who are fine. Aisha reads the four missed charts herself. Two were already on antibiotics from the ED. Ninety percent and right three times in ten, she says slowly. I'll take that, if the four still show up somewhere.

That's the move. Interpret outcomes from the two by two table, not one number. Sensitivity, specificity, and PPV trade off. Test a change on the same data, look at the cases it misses one by one, and decide with clinicians which tradeoff is safe.
Tuesday the ED medical director called before Maria had her coat off. He'd seen the pilot dashboard.
Sepsis alert override rate by unit, first fourteen days. Percent of alerts answered Not clinically indicated. The alert fired 2,280 times on the three units and was overridden 2,052 times.
Ninety-four percent, he said. You promised you'd count them honestly. There it is. Take my department out.
An hour later Tasha Greene forwarded a list without comment: sixty-three service desk tickets in two weeks from the three units, most of them some version of the same words. Alert won't go away.
A. Take the ED out of the pilot, since its override rate is the worst of the three.
B. Report only the overall override rate of ninety percent, without the unit split.
C. Have the ED help review a sample of its overrides to see which were already treated.
D. Have the ED staff retrained on sepsis, since they're overriding nearly every alert.

An ED nurse educator and Kiran pull a hundred ED overrides at random. In seventy-one, the patient had already screened positive at triage and had antibiotics ordered when the alert fired. The alert was right and the nurse was right to override it. The new rule from Thursday's change board, no repeat while the order set is active, already covers most of them. The ED director goes through the sample chart by chart. So my nurses were right. Seventy-one times out of a hundred.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. An override rate needs interpreting. Sample the overrides and ask whether each one was appropriate. A redundant alert gets overridden correctly, and the fix is to suppress it when the patient is already being treated.
Friday afternoon an email came in from Brett Talbot, Corvane's account executive, with an exclamation point in the subject line.

An email from Brett Talbot. Subject: Sepsis!. Maria, heard about your pilot. Corvane Sepsis Predict ships in your April upgrade, included in your license. It scores every inpatient every fifteen minutes. Area under the curve of 0.87 across forty customer sites. Want me to have our team switch it on for your three pilot units? Happy to bring our data scientists out to Greeley.
Aisha forwarded it back within ten minutes. 0.87 beats anything I wrote.

Marcus, copied because the model would read from lab feeds, sent one line. Model reads lactate by code. Greeley's lab got a new analyzer in October and the lactate code changed. Ask them which one it's looking for.
A. Switch it on to replace Aisha's rule, since its accuracy already beats hers.
B. Decline predictive models, since nobody can see how they arrive at their scores.
C. Run it silently on Cascade patients, compare to chart review, then decide.
D. Accept the vendor's validation, but turn it on in just one pilot unit at first.

Brett's team agrees to run it silently after the April upgrade, scores hidden from users, compared against the residents' chart review. Marcus's lactate code goes on the list to fix first. Maria asks for the results by site and by month, and for a named owner at Cascade to check it every quarter after that. Brett is a little deflated. Most customers just turn it on. I know, she says.

Exactly right. Predictive models need local validation, often in silent mode, before go-live. After go-live they need monitoring for drift, by site and over time, with an owner. A changed lab code is exactly the kind of data drift that quietly breaks a model.
Monday, March 1. The council would meet Wednesday, and Aisha wanted to open with good news. She sent Maria the chart she planned to show.
Minutes from sepsis criteria to first antibiotic, pilot units, weekly median. Twelve weeks before the pilot, then the three pilot weeks. The median of the twelve baseline weeks is 181 minutes.
From 181 to 138, she wrote. Forty-three minutes faster. I want to say the alert did it.
A. Wait to show the council anything until all thirty days of data are in.
B. Show the run chart, call it early, and keep plotting with balancing measures.
C. Present the drop from 181 to 138 minutes to the council as the pilot's result.
D. Compare the pilot weeks' average with the same weeks of last year instead.

Maria redraws it with the median line. Three points below it, all of them better than any baseline week. Promising, and not a shift until six in a row. She adds two balancing measures beside it: broad-spectrum antibiotic starts and blood cultures drawn, both flat so far. Aisha sighs. So I say promising. You say promising, and in three weeks you might say more.

That's the move. Interpret outcomes over time. A run chart with a median line and simple rules tells you whether a change is signal or noise. Three points aren't a shift. Track balancing measures so an improvement doesn't hide harm somewhere else.

That night, March 1, Rawlins started remote order verification. At 7:12 PM a Cheyenne pharmacist verified the first Rawlins night order from 150 miles away, a dose of antibiotic for a woman with a kidney infection, and the Rawlins nurse scanned it at 7:31.
Gail called Maria at 9 PM from her office at Rawlins. She sounded like she'd been waiting a year to make the call, which she had.
First night, she said. How will we know it's working? And tell me the truth. My nurses are scared a pharmacist in Cheyenne is going to make a septic patient wait for his first antibiotic.
A. Count the orders Cheyenne verifies each night, and report the volume monthly.
B. Call it a success once night override pulls drop, since that was the gap.
C. Survey the Rawlins nurses after ninety days on how the change is going.
D. Track verified-before-given, scan rate, and first dose times against baseline.

Kiran builds it from the eMAR that week. Three numbers, nights only, against last year's: first doses verified before they were given, which had been zero since the pharmacist retired; BCMA scan compliance, sitting at 62; and order to first dose for antibiotics. Pharmacy sets a rule for STAT antibiotics too. The nurse can still pull on override, and the pharmacist calls back within fifteen minutes. Gail hears all of it and lets out a breath. Okay. That I can tell them.

Good. That's what I'd want from a flight director. Judge a technology trend by outcomes against a baseline. Measure the gap it was meant to close, the knock-on effect you expect, and the risk it might create. Telepharmacy should improve safety without slowing urgent first doses.

The council met Wednesday morning, March 3. Maria and Aisha presented together: the two by two table, the override sample, the run chart, the man from Kersey, who'd gone home Saturday with his hat on. Brooke had asked to come. She sat in the back row in scrubs with her badge turned around.
Version two was ready to build. The question was how it should reach the nurse.
A. Show the broad screen on the board, and interrupt only when the tight rule hits.
B. Make version two a pop-up, and drop the broader screen altogether.
C. Make version two a hard stop that requires a lactate order before charting.
D. Keep version one, and add a mandatory sepsis module to annual training.

Two tiers. Patients who meet two vital sign criteria show up in a sepsis column on the unit board, where the charge nurse sees them every hour. That way the four patients the tighter rule missed still show up somewhere. The tighter rule fires a pop-up to the assigned nurse, with the values, the order set, and a button to call rapid response. No repeat while treatment's underway. The council approves it for all of Greeley in April, then the rest of the Corvane hospitals by summer, with monthly review. Aisha asks for a frontline nurse on the review. Brooke raises her hand from the back row.

Exactly right. Match the format to the job. A broad, low-precision screen fits a passive display. A high-precision rule earns an interruption, sent to the person who can act, with the next step built in. Monitor it after go-live.
The council voted at 10:40, and nobody voted no. The ED director abstained, which Aisha said afterward was the warmest thing he'd ever done for her.
On the way out, Greeley's director of nursing stopped Maria at the door. First alert in three years my nurses asked to keep, she said. Don't make me regret saying that out loud.

Brooke caught her in the hallway. She'd turned her badge back around. The man from Kersey. Bev said he came by 4 West to say goodbye before he went home. I was off. She held out her phone. On it was a photo Bev had sent, an old man in a hospital gown and a gray felt hat, holding up a thumb.

It had been a month of being wrong in useful ways. Aisha had been wrong about the threshold and right about the problem. Maria had been right about the pilot and slow to see how many alerts were already on those units. A first-year nurse had been wrong about one patient, and the system had been built so that the next wrong call would cost less. That was the job now: building something that held at 2 AM when somebody got it wrong.
Lucia was at the kitchen table that night with her laptop open to a nursing school application. The essay prompt was at the top of the screen. Describe a time you were wrong, and what you learned.
What's yours? Lucia said. And don't say you were never wrong.
I built an alert this month that a nurse didn't trust, Maria said. She was mostly right not to. A man almost died, and then he went home in his hat.
Lucia gave her the look she'd had since she was four, the one that meant the real answer was somewhere behind the one she got. That's not the one, though.
Will you tell me the real one?

Maria thought about Greeley, her first year, and a page that wasn't there. Not tonight, she said. Lucia rolled her eyes and went back to typing. But she'd heard the difference between not tonight and never, and so had Maria.
Her phone rang at 9:40. Ochoa never called at night.

The board's executive committee met tonight, he said. They've read the Rawlins restatement. Sixty-two percent, a year of it, at a hospital we told them was at ninety-eight. They want to know if One Chart fixes it, what it costs, and what happens if we don't do it.

In thirty days. Real numbers, Maria. Glenn's kind of numbers, not Aisha's kind. NPV, payback, and every benefit with a baseline under it. He paused. You've spent two months learning what the numbers we already had were hiding. Now you get to make new ones. Don't round anything up.

He hung up. Maria looked at the calendar on the refrigerator. Thirty days put it at the first week of April. She pulled a legal pad out of the drawer by the phone and wrote one line at the top. What does it cost to keep MedaLink?
